steps.observation: Write a short story about a lighthouse keeper.

steps.action:
The foghorn sounded just before dawn, a long, mournful note that rolled over the black water and up the ragged cliffs. Amos Reed woke to it as he always did, before the second blast, before the gulls’ thin cries cut the morning in two.

He lay for a moment in the narrow bed beneath the round window, listening to the sea breathing against the rocks, to the soft ticking of the clock on the wall, to the quiet that only existed at the edge of the world. Then he swung his legs to the floor, his bare feet finding the cold, familiar stone.

The lighthouse had three rooms: the kitchen at the base, the sleeping nook pressed into the curve of the middle level, and above that the lantern room with its glass walls and brass fittings that needed near-constant tending. Amos could move through it all with his eyes closed, and often did in winter when the glass frosted and the wind drove needles of ice under the door.

He boiled water on the small gas stove, spooned coffee grounds from the tin, and watched the flame as he waited. The fog pressed against the single oval window like damp cotton. Somewhere below, the waves worried the bones of old wrecks, splintered hulls swallowed and forgotten before his time.

He drank his coffee black, standing, as the first grey light began to thin the darkness. It was nearly time.

The climb to the lantern room was a tight spiral of iron steps worn smooth by a century of boots. Halfway up, Amos paused, as he always did, at the framed photograph bolted to the curved wall: a younger man in uniform, standing stiffly next to a girl who had his eyes and his stubborn jaw. Her hair was pulled back in a wild ponytail. Behind them, the sea was bright and harmless.

“Morning, Mae,” he murmured, as he always did, and then continued upward.

The light was his responsibility. Not just the massive Fresnel lens, a hundred years old and polished to a crystalline gleam, but the bulb, the backup bulb, the wiring, the weight-driven rotation system, the glass panes that took the full fury of every storm. Ships depended on the beam that swept from this highest point on the headland. Lives depended on it. That had been enough, once, to anchor him here.

He checked the fuel reserves for the generator, wiped a fingerprint from the lens with a soft cloth, and logged the morning inspection in tight, neat handwriting in the ledger that had outlived three keepers. Outside, the foghorn moaned again.

Ten miles offshore, hidden by the mist, the shipping lane cut a dark seam through the water. On clear days Amos could watch hulking container ships crawl along it, stacked with colored boxes like a child’s toys. Sometimes, at night, he’d hear the distant hum of their engines through the open hatch as he lay in bed, a reminder that the world beyond his island moved and shifted and did not wait for him.

He had been here twelve years. Long enough that the mainland had faded in his mind to a collection of impressions: the sour smell of the subway, his daughter’s posters on her bedroom wall, the taste of takeout noodles eaten from the carton at the kitchen table. Long enough that he could almost forget the sound of the phone ringing in the middle of the night, the silence that had poured over him when he answered, the way everything that followed had felt oddly distant, like it was happening behind glass.

Mae had been seventeen. Running a red light. No other cars involved.

The Coast Guard had offered the position at the lighthouse a few months later, when his commanding officer had quietly suggested that shore duty might be best. They needed someone steady, someone meticulous, someone who understood that sometimes the only thing between a sailor and being swallowed whole was a light on a rock and a man who would not let it go dark.

“Be good work for you, Reed,” the officer had said, not quite meeting his eyes. “Quiet. Important.”

It was. It was both.

The fog thickened as the day wore on, muting the world to shades of white and steel. Amos listened to the radio crackle with coordinates and calm, practiced voices. Midday, the supply boat’s engine shuddered through the water, the small craft emerging from the clouds with its familiar blue hull. He watched from the catwalk as it nudged the small wooden dock at the base of the cliff, the two crewmen climbing up the slick ladder with the ease of long practice.

They brought fuel, crates of canned food, fresh batteries, a sack of mail. One of them, Luis, carried a cardboard box with fresh bread from the town’s only bakery. “Mrs. Hargrove says you’ll forget how to chew if you keep living on tins,” he called as Amos met him halfway down the path carved into the cliff.

“I send her money,” Amos said, taking the box. “She sends unsolicited advice.”

“Yeah, she does that.” Luis grinned. “You got a letter this time, too. Looks personal.”

Amos tried not to show how his chest tightened at the sight of the envelope. The handwriting on the front was neat and unfamiliar, the ink slightly smudged at one corner. He turned it over and over in his hands as they moved crates from the dock to the lighthouse, as they joked about the weather, as they double-checked the manifest against his list.

“Storm blowing in tomorrow,” Luis said, squinting at the thickening fog. “Big one, they say. You got everything you need out here?”

“Always do,” Amos said.

After they left, the small boat swallowed by the wall of white, Amos sat at the table in the base of the lighthouse with the envelope in front of him. It had been years since any letter had arrived that wasn’t an official notice, a maintenance reminder, a pension form. He read the return address three times before his hands stopped shaking enough to open it.

It was from Mae’s best friend, Holly.

They had been inseparable as teenagers, loud and certain and full of plans. He remembered them sprawled on the living room floor, headphones shared between them, laughing at things they never explained. He remembered Holly’s red-rimmed eyes at the funeral, the way she had hugged him so hard it hurt.

Dear Mr. Reed, the letter began.

He read every word, slowly, twice.

She wrote that she had been thinking of Mae. That she had found an old photo, the three of them on the boardwalk, the ocean behind them, a gull frozen mid-flight in the corner of the frame. That she had a daughter now, three years old, named May—not spelled the same, Holly apologized, but it was for her, all the same. That she had thought of calling a hundred times and never had.

I guess I’m writing because I wanted you to know, she wrote. She mattered. To me, to a lot of people. Not just in the way something is sad when it’s gone, but in the way it changes you while it’s there. I still hear her in my head sometimes, saying I’m being too cautious, that I should just go. She would hate that I haven’t told you about my May. So I’m telling you.

I hope you’re okay out there with your lighthouse. Mae always said it sounded like something from a story, you know. A man on a rock with a big light, saving ships. She was proud of you, even when she pretended not to be.

Amos folded the letter carefully and stared at the wall until the clock ticked their way into late afternoon. The fog dulled the daylight to a permanent twilight. The brass of the lantern fittings had taken on a bloodless sheen.

That night, the storm arrived earlier than predicted.

He felt it first as a subtle shift in the wind’s pitch, a lower, more insistent note under the usual howl. The barometer needle refused to settle. By the time he climbed to the lantern room to begin the evening routine, rain had begun to lash the glass in fast, furious bursts.

He lit the main bulb and watched as the beam leapt into the dark, carving a bright path through the storm. The mechanism hummed, turning the lens at its patient pace, sending the light across the black water: a white flash every ten seconds, seventy miles of warning in each pulse.

The radio crackled with weather updates, storm advisories. A fishing trawler requested permission to alter course, a response came, clipped and professional. None of it was his to answer; his job—his whole job—was to keep the light burning and the horn sounding.

By midnight, the storm had become a living thing.

Wind slammed against the tower with both hands. The waves struck the base in great, booming impacts that shuddered up through the stone, rattling the shelves. The glass of the lantern room trembled. Amos checked and rechecked the seals around each pane, watching for leaks, for fractures, for any sign that the century-old structure might be tired enough at last to give in.

He was tightening a bolt at the base of the rotation mechanism when he noticed it: a hitch.

The light stuttered. A fraction of a second, a subtle pause in the smooth, regular sweep. He felt it more than saw it, the way a man who has lived for years by the rhythm of the sea can feel the wrongness of a single wave.

He watched the next rotation, counting under his breath. One, two, three, four—

The motor gave a cramped little jerk. The light slowed, then righted itself. Somewhere down in the depths of the machinery, a worn gear was slipping.

“Not tonight,” he said aloud.

He cut power to the motor, the mechanism grinding to a sullen halt. The beam froze pointing north, painting the heaving water with a stark white stripe. Without rotation, the lighthouse became a single unblinking eye, less useful, less visible to ships rounding the headland from the south.

The backup system was a hand-cranked weight mechanism, heavy brass and iron that had not been used in a storm of this magnitude since long before Amos’s time. He had tested it in calm weather, taken notes, oiled the joints. He had promised himself he would be ready if it failed. Standing there with the storm clawing at the windows, he felt suddenly very small.

He released the weight, listening to it descend with a slow, ponderous clunk. The mechanism engaged, gears meshing, the great lens beginning its deliberate turn once more. The beam swept through the rain in a slow arc.

The old system would work as long as he kept resetting the weight. It needed to be rewound every thirty minutes. If he forgot, if he slept, if he slipped—

He checked the clock. 12:17.

Down below, something crashed to the floor, a casualty of the tower’s shuddering. He ignored it. He noted the time in the log. He watched the light complete a full rotation, then another. The storm howled on.

At 12:47, he rewound the weight.

At 1:17, he did it again. His shoulders ached from the effort, a deep, grinding pull in muscles that had gone soft with age and isolation.

He thought of Mae on the boardwalk, her hair whipped by the wind, face tilted up to the harsh winter sun.

“This place would be better with storms,” she had said once, bored by the flat November sky. “I like when it feels like something is happening.”

“Bad weather doesn’t care what you like,” he’d told her. “It just is. That’s the point.”

“Spoken like a man who never learned to have fun,” she’d said, bumping her shoulder into his. “Come on, Dad. At least pretend.”

He smiled without meaning to as he leaned his weight into the crank. The tower creaked in protest around him.

At 1:38, the radio snapped to urgent life.

“—Coast Guard, this is the trawler Evermore, do you copy? We have engine failure, repeat, engine failure. Coordinates—”

Amos scribbled them in the margin of the log, numbers and degrees slipping slightly under his pen. Twelve miles southeast, near the reef that had broken three ships in the last fifty years. Too close. Far too close in a storm like this.

“Evermore, this is Station Four,” came the calm reply. “We copy. Maintain position if able. Rescue vessel en route, ETA forty minutes.”

“Negative on maintaining,” the trawler’s captain said, his voice thin and strained beneath the static. “We’re drifting. I… we can’t see the light. Visibility’s—”

The transmission cut out, swallowed by a burst of interference.

Amos looked sharply at the clock. 1:39. The light finished its slow rotation, throwing its beam southward across the teeth of the reef.

He pictured the trawler, a dark shape shoved sideways by the heaving sea, powerless, blind. The thought came quick and sharp, a statement rather than a question: If they can’t see the light, they’ll hit the rocks.

He knew the charts by heart. He knew, as intimately as he knew the lines on his own palms, the way the currents curled and twisted around the headland. In a storm like this, the wind would push them toward the reef at a brutal pace. Forty minutes was too long.

He checked the lantern. The flame was strong. The lens turned, steady, dutiful. Perhaps the visibility really was just that poor. Perhaps he was doing everything that could be done.

He thought of all the times he had told himself exactly that, over other things, in other lives.

He moved without deciding to. Down the spiral stairs, past the photograph. Past his bed, the covers still twisted from when he’d left them hours earlier. Down to the base, where the wind found its way under the door and made the lamp flame tremble.

In the small equipment room, he opened a long, narrow locker. Inside, wrapped in oilcloth, was a flare gun and eight red cylinders. He checked each one with fingers that had somehow gone numb. All expired by a year. Regulations said they should have been replaced. He had requested new ones every quarter, signed the forms, mailed them off with practiced precision. Somewhere in a budget office, someone had decided the old ones would do a little longer.

He loaded one into the gun. Slipped three more into his jacket pocket. Took a coil of rope from its hook.

The catwalk around the lantern room was a small, exposed ring of metal, ten stories above the churning sea. The wind hit him like a physical blow when he forced the hatch open. For a moment, he had to cling to the frame just to stay upright, rain stinging his face, his breath ripped from his lungs.

The world beyond was chaos. The beam of the lighthouse cut a clean path through the rain, a bright blade sweeping across an ocean that looked more like shattered slate than water. He squinted into the darkness, eyes straining, and saw nothing but endless, heaving black.

He secured the rope around the thick base of the lantern housing and tied the other end around his waist. It felt absurd; if he went over, the wind and water would tear him like paper. But the knotwork was something he could control, something he could perfect.

The first flare arced into the sky with a hiss, momentarily brighter than the lighthouse itself. It rose, streaked red against the storm, then burst into a brilliant, floating bloom of light high above the water. For a minute, the world was revealed in stark, bloody detail: the crests of waves like white claws, the jagged line of the reef, the faint, rolling shape of a vessel where no vessel should be, dangerously close to the teeth of rock.

“There you are,” Amos said under his breath, though the wind stole the words as soon as they left his mouth.

The flare sputtered and died, plunging the world back into darkness. The lighthouse beam continued its steady, impartial rotation.

He fired another, aiming slightly farther east. The brief red sun burst overhead, and he saw the trawler again, a little farther from the reef this time. The change was small, but it was there, a subtle shift of angle.

They had seen him.

The storm did not pause to acknowledge this. The next gust nearly wrenched him from his feet. The rope around his waist went taut, cutting into his ribs. He braced himself against the railing, his fingers numb on the wet metal.

He kept firing.

Between each flare, he ducked back into the lantern room long enough to wind the weight again, the mechanism groaning in a rhythm that matched the pounding in his chest. His arms screamed. His legs shook.

He thought of Mae leaning over a textbook, pronouncing “littoral” with exaggerated care as she studied for a quiz on coastal geography.

“Imagine it’s you,” she’d said, eyes flashing with mischief. “Litorally a man in a lighthouse. Littoral lighthouse man.”

He had tried not to laugh. Failed. She had looked so pleased.

The fifth flare misfired.

He felt the soft, sickly click instead of the sharp, satisfying snap. The cylinder lodged half-in, half-out of the chamber. For a second, he saw the future contained in that small mechanical failure: the flare going off in his hands, his fingers shredded, blood lost to the wind and rain before he could even scream.

He set the gun down carefully on the catwalk. His hands were trembling, whether from cold or adrenaline or age he could not say. The last flare felt ridiculously small and heavy in his pocket.

He took a breath as deep as the air would allow, tasting metal and salt. Inside the lantern room, the clock ticked toward the next winding. He could not see it, but he felt its presence, insistent, in the back of his mind.

He fired the final flare straight up.

It rose more slowly than the others, as though reluctant to leave. When it burst, the light seemed to hang in the sky forever, a defiant red star in a world of black and grey.

In that light, the entire scene was revealed: the screaming surf, the hungry reef, the trawler edging, inch by inch, into the narrow channel that would carry it clear of the rocks if it held that course and no crueler gust of wind shoved it astray.

He saw, just for a second, tiny figures on the deck, heads turned toward the impossible man on the impossible rock, the flare gun raised in his shaking hand. He wondered if any of them would remember this night years from now, tell the story in a bar somewhere.

“We were done for,” they’d say, maybe. “Couldn’t see a thing. Then we saw this light—no, not the lighthouse, something red, up high, and there he was…”

The flare dwindled, dimmed, died.

Darkness crushed in again, thick and absolute.

He went inside. He wound the weight. The lighthouse turned.

On the radio, twenty minutes later, the Evermore’s captain reported that they had cleared the reef.

“Still dead in the water,” he said, voice shaking now that the worst had passed. “But holding steady. We saw flares from the headland. Wouldn’t have made the gap without them. Thank you.”

“Copy that, Evermore,” came the reply. “Rescue vessel ETA ten minutes. Stand by.”

No one
